case_analysis.focal_point: Whether ATF’s 2018 rule classifying bump-stock devices as “machineguns” is a lawful interpretation of federal law—i.e., whether a semiautomatic rifle equipped with a bump stock “shoots … automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger” under the National Firearms Act and Gun Control Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b) (National Firearms Act definition of “machinegun”), incorporated via 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(23), and related criminal prohibitions/penalties under 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) and 26 U.S.C. § 5861.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The government argues that bump stocks enable a firearm to fire multiple rounds automatically with a single trigger function because, once the shooter initiates the firing sequence and maintains constant pressure, the device harnesses recoil so the gun continues firing without additional deliberate trigger pulls; in the government’s view, the statutory terms “automatically” and “single function of the trigger” encompass this continuous, self-acting firing cycle, so ATF’s rule correctly treats bump stocks as machineguns and should be upheld.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Cargill argues the statute unambiguously excludes bump stocks because the rifle still fires only one round per trigger movement/activation and requires repeated trigger functions as the trigger physically resets and re-engages; he also contends that even if there were ambiguity, courts should not defer to an agency’s interpretation of a criminal statute (invoking rule-of-lenity/separation-of-powers concerns), and that ATF’s reversal from earlier positions further undermines any claim to deference or persuasive weight.
key_precedents: Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc. (1984)
Baldwin v. United States (2020) (Thomas, J., dissenting from denial of certiorari)
Guedes v. ATF (D.C. Cir. 2019) (referenced in the quoted excerpt as “Guedes II”)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s volitional account—once constant pressure is applied, successive shots occur without additional intentional trigger pulls—has intuitive force in ordinary speech, and it squarely presses the word “automatically.” But as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 5845(b) does not define “machinegun” by the shooter’s subjective volition; it ties “automatically” to a specific mechanical criterion: “more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” and the trigger’s reset and re-engagement between rounds makes it, at minimum, unclear that one trigger function yields multiple shots. Given that this definition is embedded in a criminally enforceable regime (§ 922(o), § 5861), Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers/lenity point and Thompson/Center Arms counsel against allowing ATF’s reversal to supply the needed clarity where Congress has not spoken plainly. A narrow disposition—holding only that the statute does not clearly authorize treating bump stocks as machineguns—best preserves institutional legitimacy and leaves the policy question to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best argument is that a bump stock yields successive shots without additional volitional trigger pulls once constant pressure is applied, so it seems “automatic” in ordinary speech. But § 5845(b) does not ask about the shooter’s volition; as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, it makes a mechanical inquiry—whether the firearm shoots “more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger”—and with a bump stock the trigger must reset and be re-engaged between each shot, so there is not more than one shot per trigger function. Even if Sotomayor’s reading were plausible, this is a criminally enforceable definition, and Thompson/Center Arms plus our separation-of-powers cases (as Roberts notes via Abramski/Apel) require that any genuine interpretive doubt be resolved by courts and, ultimately, lenity—not by an agency’s reversal expanding criminal liability. Congress may reach bump stocks if it chooses, but the text it enacted does not clearly do so.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest argument is that, in ordinary terms, a bump stock makes the firearm fire “automatically” once the shooter maintains constant pressure, so “single function” could be read as the shooter’s single initiating act. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the statute’s operative limiter is not volition in general; it is the mechanical criterion “more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” and the trigger must reset and be re-engaged for each round, making the Government’s reading at least strained. Even if Sotomayor’s broader reading is plausible in isolation, Thompson/Center Arms (as Justice Thomas notes) and the serious criminal penalties counsel that any residual uncertainty cannot be resolved by agency expansion and instead triggers lenity and separation-of-powers limits. Abramski and Apel reinforce that courts must fix the meaning of criminal statutes and should not permit the Executive to enlarge criminal liability absent clear congressional authorization.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers/lenity point seriously, but it presupposes that § 5845(b) remains genuinely ambiguous after ordinary textual analysis; in my view it does not. Their trigger-reset framing (echoed by Justice Thomas) treats “single function of the trigger” as a purely internal mechanical event, yet the more natural reading—consistent with how Congress used “automatically” in defining machineguns—is that one continuous, shooter-initiated trigger function (a single initiating act maintained under constant pressure) that sets in motion recoil-driven, self-acting fire counts as “single function,” even if the mechanism cycles. Thompson/Center Arms and Abramski/Apel underscore that courts must fix the meaning and that lenity can apply, but those cases do not require lenity when text, context, and statutory purpose converge on coverage; here, the device is designed to make the firearm fire successive shots without additional volitional trigger manipulation in the ordinary sense. I agree with Justice Kagan that Chevron has no role and that ATF’s reversal deserves little weight, but independent judicial interpretation still supports the petitioner, so I would not shift the criminal-liability line solely because the Executive changed its mind.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best argument is that, from the shooter’s perspective, maintaining constant pressure initiates a recoil-driven sequence with no additional volitional trigger pulls, so “automatically” seems to fit in ordinary language. But the statute does not hinge on volition; it defines “machinegun” in mechanical terms—“more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger”—and, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the trigger must reset and be re-engaged between rounds on a bump stock, making it at least not clearly within that text. Roberts’s Abramski/Apel separation-of-powers point and Justice Thomas’s Thompson/Center Arms lenity point matter to my pragmatic textualism because they counsel against letting an agency reversal supply the clarity Congress did not provide in a criminally enforceable definition. On this record, the most coherent, administrable line is to hold ATF lacked clear statutory authorization and leave any expansion to Congress.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point—that a bump stock yields sustained fire without additional volitional trigger pulls and so sounds “automatic” in ordinary speech—does not answer the statute Congress wrote, which ties “automatically” to the mechanism: “more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger.” As Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan emphasize, the trigger must reset and be mechanically re-engaged between shots, so each round follows a new trigger function rather than multiple shots from one. Even if Sotomayor’s volition-based reading of “single function” is linguistically possible, Chief Justice Roberts is right that in a criminally enforced regime we do not permit the Executive to supply clarity by regulatory redefinition; any remaining uncertainty is Congress’s to fix, not ATF’s. Moskal/Ocasio’s reluctance toward lenity does not overcome the separation-of-powers problem here, because those cases do not endorse letting an agency broaden the reach of criminal liability when the statutory text does not clearly do so.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s volitional account of “single function” (the shooter’s single initiating act) is the best pushback, but it asks us to detach § 5845(b)’s trigger-centric limiter from the mechanical reality that the trigger resets and is re-engaged between shots. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the statute’s operative test is “more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” and on this record there remains at least serious doubt that one trigger function yields multiple shots with a bump stock. Justice Kagan’s point about ATF’s reversal further reinforces the institutional problem of letting the Executive expand a criminally enforceable definition without clear congressional text. Given the criminal overlay and Thompson/Center Arms-style lenity concerns noted by Justice Thomas, any residual uncertainty must be resolved against the Government and left to Congress to fix.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that a bump stock looks “automatic” because the shooter maintains constant pressure without additional volitional trigger pulls—does not overcome the statute’s textual limiter: “automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” which is framed in mechanical, trigger-centered terms rather than the shooter’s ongoing intent. As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the trigger must reset and be re-engaged between shots, so each discharge follows a distinct trigger function even if the shooter’s pressure is continuous. Chief Justice Roberts’s separation-of-powers point reinforces my view that, in a criminally enforced scheme, we should not treat an agency’s post hoc, reversed interpretation as supplying the clarity Congress did not provide, and Justice Thomas’s Thompson/Center Arms lenity framing confirms that any remaining doubt about the NFA definition should be resolved against expanding criminal liability. Under original public meaning and our precedent on notice and institutional roles, the policy argument for covering bump stocks is for Congress, not ATF, to implement.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that in ordinary usage a bump-stock-equipped firearm seems to fire “automatically” once constant pressure is maintained—has real intuitive force, and I take seriously her Moskal/Ocasio warning against invoking lenity too quickly. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 5845(b) is not a free-floating “automatic” standard; it narrows the definition to firing “more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” and the mechanical reset/re-engagement between shots makes the Government’s reading at least uncertain on the statute’s own terms. Given the severe criminal consequences under § 922(o) and § 5861 and the agency’s interpretive reversal, I agree with Justice Thomas (Thompson/Center Arms) that any residual uncertainty cannot be resolved by administrative expansion of criminal liability, consistent with the procedural-fairness and notice values that animate lenity. That combination—textual limiter plus criminal-law notice concerns—keeps me with the respondent.

John Roberts.reasoning: The question is one of statutory interpretation of 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b), which imposes serious criminal consequences through 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) and 26 U.S.C. § 5861, and we should not lightly allow an agency to expand that definition by regulation. At minimum, the statutory phrase “automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger” does not clearly encompass a device where the trigger mechanically resets and is re-engaged between shots, and that uncertainty triggers the rule-of-lenity principle that courts, not the Executive, define the scope of criminal liability. Our precedents caution against deference in this setting—see Abramski v. United States, 573 U.S. 169, 191 (2014) (“criminal laws are for courts, not for the Government, to construe”) and INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca (1987) (declining to defer where the statute’s meaning is for the courts to say). A narrow, institutionally cautious disposition is to hold only that ATF lacked clear statutory authorization to treat bump stocks as “machineguns,” leaving any policy change to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The statutory text defines a “machinegun” as a weapon that “shoots … automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b), and a bump-stock-equipped semiautomatic rifle still fires only one round per trigger cycle as the trigger resets between shots. Even if the Government can posit a plausible alternative reading of “single function” or “automatically,” this is a criminal-enforcement scheme (18 U.S.C. § 922(o); 26 U.S.C. § 5861), and ambiguity must be resolved for the accused under the rule of lenity rather than by agency redefinition. Thompson/Center Arms confirms lenity’s application to the NFA’s definitional provisions, and Chevron-style deference is inappropriate where an agency interpretation would expand criminal liability. Accordingly, ATF’s 2018 rule exceeds the best reading of the statute and cannot be sustained.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The statutory text defines a “machinegun” as a weapon that shoots “automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b), and a bump-stock-equipped semiautomatic rifle still fires only one round per trigger function because the trigger must reset and re-engage for each shot. Even if the government’s reading were plausible, this interpretation would expand conduct subject to serious criminal liability under 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) and 26 U.S.C. § 5861, and courts should not apply Chevron-style deference to an agency’s interpretation of a criminal statute. As Justice Scalia explained, Babbitt’s “drive-by” deference in a criminally enforceable context deserves little weight, Whitman v. United States (Scalia, J., respecting denial of certiorari), and we owe an independent judicial determination before the Government may impose criminal punishment. Given the rule-of-lenity/separation-of-powers concerns and the statute’s best reading, ATF’s 2018 rule is not a lawful interpretation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Reading 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b) in context, a bump stock enables a rifle to “shoot[] … automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger” because, once the shooter initiates the firing sequence and maintains constant pressure, recoil-driven mechanics allow successive rounds to fire without any additional volitional trigger act, fitting the ordinary meaning of “automatically.” Even setting Chevron aside given the criminal consequences, the Court can resolve the question through the traditional tools of statutory construction without finding the “grievous ambiguity” required to invoke lenity under Moskal v. United States and Ocasio v. United States. Fair notice and separation-of-powers concerns are real, but they do not justify adopting an artificially cramped reading that would exempt a device engineered to mimic continuous fire and thereby undermine Congress’s machinegun restrictions in § 5845(b) and the related prohibitions in 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) and 26 U.S.C. § 5861. On balance, the practical, life-and-death harms to vulnerable communities from rapid-fire weaponry support upholding ATF’s classification where the statutory text can reasonably bear that construction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 5845(b) defines a “machinegun” as a weapon that shoots “automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” and that text most naturally focuses on the trigger’s operative function—i.e., whether one trigger function yields multiple shots without intervening trigger functions. With a bump stock, each shot still depends on the trigger resetting and being actuated again as the rifle reciprocates, so the better reading is that the firearm does not fire more than one shot “by a single function of the trigger” within the statute’s terms. Even if the statute were ambiguous, the rule carries criminal prohibitions and penalties under 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) and 26 U.S.C. § 5861, and Chevron-style deference is especially ill-suited in criminal-adjacent contexts; in addition, ATF’s sharp reversal from earlier views counsels against deference under INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca, 480 U.S. 421, 446 n.30 (1987), and Epic Systems’ skepticism when “the Executive seems of two minds.”

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 5845(b) defines a “machinegun” as a weapon that “shoots … automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” and the best reading of that text focuses on what the trigger does: with a bump stock, the trigger still resets and is actuated each time the firearm fires a round, yielding (at most) one shot per trigger function rather than multiple shots by one trigger function. Even if the statutory terms “automatically” or “single function of the trigger” admitted doubt, this is a criminally enforced regime (18 U.S.C. § 922(o); 26 U.S.C. § 5861), and the Executive may not expand criminal liability by regulation; “the Government’s reading of a criminal statute is [not] entitled to any deference,” United States v. Apel, 571 U.S. 359, 369 (2014), and “criminal laws are for courts, not for the Government, to construe,” Abramski v. United States, 573 U.S. 169, 191 (2014). Separation-of-powers principles and the rule of lenity thus require rejecting ATF’s 2018 rule as an impermissible rewriting of § 5845(b), leaving any policy change to Congress.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b), a “machinegun” must “shoot[] … automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” and with a bump stock the trigger still resets and functions repeatedly—one shot per trigger function—so the better reading is that the statute does not cover bump stocks. Even if the statutory terms admitted some ambiguity, this is a criminal-prohibition scheme enforced through 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) and 26 U.S.C. § 5861, so courts should not “place [a] thumb on the scale in favor of the government” via deference; the Court has emphasized that “criminal laws are for courts, not for the Government, to construe.” The ATF’s reversal from prior interpretations also undercuts any claim to persuasive weight and raises rule-of-law and reliance concerns, favoring judicial restraint and leaving any expansion of criminal liability to Congress. Consistent with Abramski and Apel, I would interpret the statute using traditional tools and, at minimum, apply the rule of lenity against the Government’s broader reading.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The relevant text defines a “machinegun” as a weapon that “shoots … automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b), and a semiautomatic rifle with a bump stock still fires only one round per trigger function because the trigger must reset and re-engage for each shot. Even if the statute admitted some uncertainty about “single function” or “automatically,” courts should not resolve that uncertainty by deferring to an agency interpretation that expands criminal liability under 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) and 26 U.S.C. § 5861, particularly given separation-of-powers and lenity concerns reflected in the Court’s reluctance to apply Chevron in criminal contexts. The agency’s abrupt reversal from prior positions further weakens any claim to deference or persuasive weight, consistent with INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca’s observation that interpretations conflicting with an agency’s earlier view deserve “considerably less deference.” Methodologically, the better course is to adhere to the statute’s ordinary meaning and leave any expansion of criminal prohibitions to Congress, not ATF rulemaking.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The statutory definition in 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b) turns on whether the weapon shoots “automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” and a bump-stock-equipped semiautomatic rifle still fires only one round per trigger cycle as the trigger resets and re-engages between shots. Because the ATF’s rule would expand the scope of conduct subject to serious criminal penalties under 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) and 26 U.S.C. § 5861, procedural fairness counsels against adopting an agency interpretation that effectively defines new criminal liability through regulation rather than clear congressional text. Consistent with this Court’s reluctance to import Chevron-style deference into criminal statutory interpretation (see INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca’s emphasis that Chevron does not govern every interpretive question, and the concerns flagged in Whitman v. United States (Scalia, J., respecting denial of certiorari)), any residual ambiguity should be resolved by the rule of lenity rather than deference. Practical consequences reinforce that separation-of-powers and notice concerns are acute where an agency reverses prior positions and then imposes criminal exposure on ordinary gun owners without unmistakable statutory authorization.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether ATF’s rule classifying bump-stock-equipped semiautomatic rifles as “machineguns” is a permissible reading of the federal statutory definition of “machinegun.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) (ban on possession/transfer of machineguns) and 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b) (National Firearms Act definition of “machinegun,” including weapons that shoot “automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The government argues that a bump stock enables a rifle to fire multiple shots automatically with a single trigger function by harnessing recoil so that, from the shooter’s perspective, the trigger is engaged once and the device causes rapid successive firing without additional volitional trigger pulls; therefore bump stocks fall within the statutory definition of “machinegun.” Petitioners also contend the rule fits Congress’s purpose in regulating weapons capable of machinegun-like rates of fire and that the agency’s interpretation is at least a reasonable construction of the statutory text (and, to the extent relevant, courts should not invalidate the rule based on a hypertechnical understanding of “trigger function” divorced from how the firearm operates with the device).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Cargill argues the statute unambiguously excludes bump stocks because, mechanically, a bump stock does not make the rifle fire more than one shot per trigger movement; instead the trigger resets and is actuated repeatedly as the gun slides back and forth, meaning each shot corresponds to a separate function of the trigger and is not “automatic” fire “by a single function of the trigger.” He further argues that ATF cannot expand criminal liability by regulation, that any ambiguity must be resolved in the defendant’s favor under the rule of lenity (rather than deference to the agency), and that ATF’s shifting positions over time underscore that the rule is not a faithful reading of the statute.
key_precedents: Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, 138 S. Ct. 1612 (2018)
Baldwin v. United States, 140 S. Ct. 690 (2020) (Thomas, J., dissenting from denial of certiorari)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is that, in practical operation, a shooter can maintain continuous pressure and obtain a sustained burst, so “single function” should be read from the user’s perspective to prevent easy evasion. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the statute Congress wrote ties the definition to the “function of the trigger,” and with a bump stock each shot still requires a distinct trigger cycle—reset and re-engagement—so the weapon does not fire more than one shot “by a single function” of that mechanism. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Apel and Abramski reinforces my separation-of-powers concern: where § 5845(b) supplies an element for § 922(o)’s criminal prohibition, we should not allow an agency’s shifting interpretation to expand liability, and any genuine residual ambiguity is for lenity, not purposive construction. A narrow holding on text/lenity (without broader pronouncements) best preserves institutional legitimacy and leaves any expansion of the machinegun definition to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that a bump stock permits a sustained burst “without additional volitional trigger pulls,” so “single function of the trigger” should be read from the shooter’s practical perspective. But the statutory text speaks to the trigger’s function, and the original public meaning of “function of the trigger” in firearms usage is the mechanical actuation event that releases the hammer/striker; with a bump stock, each shot still requires the trigger to reset and be actuated again, even if recoil assists the timing. Justice Sotomayor’s purpose-based framing cannot override the words Congress chose, especially where § 5845(b) is incorporated into § 922(o)’s criminal prohibition and thus demands clear notice; as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, any residual uncertainty belongs to the rule of lenity, not an agency’s policy-driven expansion. I therefore remain unpersuaded that the Government’s reading is the best textual/originalist reading, and I would not allow executive reinterpretation to enlarge criminal liability absent clear congressional authorization.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take seriously Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Barrett’s mechanical-cycle point that the trigger resets between shots and thus each round corresponds to a discrete actuation; if that were the ordinary meaning of “function of the trigger” in this statutory context, the Government would have a much harder case. But I am not persuaded that Congress used “function” to codify a gunsmith’s sear-reset taxonomy rather than the ordinary operational fact the statute targets—whether one continuous trigger engagement produces multiple shots automatically “without manual reloading,” which is how bump stocks are designed to mimic automatic fire from the shooter’s perspective. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Apel and Abramski appropriately rejects agency deference to expand criminal liability, yet those cases do not themselves supply the best textual meaning; they simply confirm that we must decide it, and on my reading the text is sufficiently clear to reach bump stocks without invoking lenity. Because I still see “single function” as naturally capturing a continuous trigger engagement that yields a burst, I do not think the rule of lenity is triggered here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Gorsuch and Barrett make the most serious point: because § 5845(b) feeds a criminal prohibition via § 922(o), we must be wary of agency-driven expansions and, if true ambiguity persists, lenity applies. But that concern does not decide the antecedent question of best reading; “single function of the trigger” in ordinary firearms parlance can sensibly mean a single continuous trigger engagement by the user that produces multiple shots automatically “without manual reloading,” which is exactly how bump stocks are designed to operate in real-world use. Apel and Abramski (as Justice Thomas invokes them) reinforce that courts—not ATF—must supply that best reading; they do not compel adopting an artificially mechanical definition that would let Congress’s machinegun prohibition be engineered around by exploiting reset cycles invisible to the shooter’s single, continuous input. Because I find the text, read in its practical, user-facing sense, sufficiently clear, I do not reach lenity, and separation-of-powers values are satisfied by our own construction rather than by deference to ATF.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Alito make the best counterargument: in real-world use the shooter maintains continuous pressure and the gun produces a sustained burst, so “single function” should be read in a user-facing, practical way. But the statute does not say “single pull” or “single continuous pressure”; it says “single function of the trigger,” and as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, that wording most naturally refers to the trigger’s mechanical actuation cycle—reset and re-engagement—so each shot is still not produced by a single trigger function. Their invocation of Apel and Abramski also matters to my analysis because it underscores that, where this definition supplies criminal liability via § 922(o), we should not stretch text to meet perceived purpose and we certainly should not let an agency’s policy judgment do so; any genuine residual ambiguity is resolved by lenity. On a pragmatic textualist approach, the government’s reading risks converting a trigger-focused definition into a shooter-focused one and undermines statutory coherence and notice in criminal law.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that “single function of the trigger” should be read from the shooter’s practical perspective—continuous pressure yielding a burst—and that a mechanical reading risks evasion by design. But the statutory phrase is anchored to the trigger’s function, not the shooter’s ongoing intent or pressure, and as Justice Barrett and the Chief emphasize, each round with a bump stock still requires a distinct trigger reset and re-engagement, so it is not “more than one shot … by a single function.” Even if Justice Alito is right that Congress broadly targeted automatic-burst fire, that purpose cannot supply the clear textual hook needed to expand a definition that underwrites § 922(o)’s criminal liability. And consistent with Justice Thomas’s reliance on Apel and Abramski, any genuine ambiguity in this criminally operative definition is for courts to resolve with the rule of lenity, not for ATF to resolve by regulation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Sotomayor make the best case that, from the shooter’s perspective, a bump stock allows a sustained burst with one continuous input, so “single function” should be read functionally. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch stress, Congress keyed the definition to the “function of the trigger,” a mechanical referent in ordinary firearms usage, and with a bump stock the trigger still must reset and be actuated again for each shot—recoil may facilitate the timing, but it does not collapse multiple trigger cycles into one. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Apel and Abramski reinforces that we should not allow executive reinterpretation to expand criminal liability under § 922(o) where Congress has not spoken clearly, and any genuine residual ambiguity is for lenity, not agency policymaking. Purpose and public-safety consequences cannot supply the clear notice required in a criminal statute, especially given ATF’s shifting positions, so I remain with Respondent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s shooter-centered reading usefully highlights how bump stocks achieve sustained bursts with continuous pressure, but it risks rewriting “function of the trigger” into “function of the shooter.” As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan note, the statute’s text is keyed to the trigger’s own operative cycle; with a bump stock, the trigger still resets and is re-engaged for each round, so the weapon does not fire more than one shot “by a single function of the trigger.” Justice Thomas’s reliance on Apel and Abramski strengthens the separation-of-powers point that courts must not enlarge a criminal prohibition via executive interpretation, and ATF’s shifting positions underscore the lack of clear notice. Even if Alito’s account creates some practical appeal, any residual ambiguity in a criminally operative definition must be resolved by lenity, not purposive expansion.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s user-facing account—continuous pressure producing a sustained burst—best captures the practical harm Congress had in mind, but it still asks us to rewrite “function of the trigger” into “function of the shooter,” which the statutory language does not naturally support. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the better reading ties “function” to the trigger’s operative cycle: with a bump stock, each round still depends on a reset and a subsequent actuation, even if recoil facilitates the timing. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Apel and Abramski strengthens my procedural-fairness concern that we cannot expand criminal liability through an agency’s shifting interpretations; where § 5845(b) supplies the definition for § 922(o), any remaining uncertainty must be resolved by lenity, not by purpose-driven enlargement. Public-safety consequences (highlighted by Justice Alito) are serious, but under a criminal prohibitory scheme they cannot substitute for clear legislative notice.

John Roberts.reasoning: The statutory definition in 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b) turns on whether the weapon fires “automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” and the more natural reading focuses on the trigger’s operative function for each shot rather than the shooter’s overall input or intent. Given the criminal consequences attached through 18 U.S.C. § 922(o), any genuine ambiguity about whether bump-stock-equipped rifles fit that definition should be resolved by courts, not expanded by agency rulemaking, and in close cases the rule of lenity counsels against the Government’s broader construction. Our precedents caution against importing administrative deference where it would enlarge criminal liability, and the Government’s policy arguments cannot substitute for Congress speaking clearly in the text. A narrow holding that the statute does not clearly reach bump stocks preserves institutional legitimacy by leaving any extension of the ban to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Applying the statutory text, 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b) covers only weapons that fire “automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger.” A bump stock does not change the firearm’s mechanism so that multiple rounds discharge from one trigger function; rather, the trigger resets and is actuated repeatedly as the rifle reciprocates, so each shot still corresponds to a separate trigger function. Because this interpretation bears directly on criminal liability under 18 U.S.C. § 922(o), courts owe no Chevron-style deference to an agency’s broadened reading of the statute, and any residual ambiguity must be resolved under the rule of lenity rather than in the Government’s favor. See United States v. Apel, 571 U.S. 359, 369 (2014) (no deference to the Government’s reading of a criminal statute) and Abramski v. United States, 573 U.S. 169, 191 (2014) (criminal laws are for courts to construe).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 5845(b) covers a weapon that shoots “automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger,” and a bump stock—by harnessing recoil and maintaining continuous trigger engagement—enables a sustained burst of fire without additional volitional trigger pulls, which fits the ordinary meaning of “single function” in practical operation. Reading “function” to mean each internal reset-and-release cycle is an unduly mechanical construction that would undermine Congress’s evident aim in § 922(o) to prohibit civilian possession of firearms capable of machinegun-like automatic fire. Even assuming lenity limits expansive readings of criminal statutes, the better textual reading here is that the bump-stock-equipped rifle fires multiple shots automatically during one continuous trigger function, so lenity does not control. This approach accords with the Court’s insistence on statutory text as the best evidence of meaning, see Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, 138 S. Ct. 1612 (2018), while also accounting for the real-world consequences for public safety and law enforcement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Reading 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b) in a practical, functional way, a bump stock enables a semiautomatic rifle to fire “automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger,” because the device harnesses recoil to sustain continuous firing after the shooter initiates a single trigger engagement and maintains pressure, producing machinegun-like automatic fire. That construction best serves Congress’s evident purpose in 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) to restrict weapons capable of rapid, sustained fire that magnifies the risk of mass casualty harm, especially to vulnerable populations. While the rule of lenity has an important role when Congress leaves genuine uncertainty about criminalized conduct, this text can be applied to the real-world operation of the weapon with the device without resorting to a hypertechnical trigger-mechanics focus that defeats the statute’s protective function. Consistent with INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca, we should not allow interpretive canons to override the most faithful reading of the statutory language in context, particularly where public safety consequences are substantial.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The statutory definition in 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b) turns on whether the weapon fires “automatically…by a single function of the trigger,” and the better textual reading is that a bump stock does not alter the trigger’s function so that more than one shot is fired per trigger actuation—each shot still requires the trigger to reset and be actuated again, even if recoil-assisted. Because 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) and the NFA definition carry criminal consequences, any remaining uncertainty after applying ordinary interpretive tools is resolved by the rule of lenity rather than administrative deference, consistent with Crandon v. United States and the plurality approach in United States v. Thompson/Center Arms Co. ATF’s policy aims and the device’s practical rate of fire cannot supply what the text withholds, and the agency’s shifting interpretations underscore that the statute is at least not clearly on the government’s side. On this record, the rule is not a permissible reading of § 5845(b) in a way that expands criminal liability by regulation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 5845(b) defines a “machinegun” as a weapon that shoots “automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger,” and a bump stock does not eliminate the need for repeated trigger functions; each shot occurs only after the trigger resets and is actuated again as the firearm reciprocates. Even if the government’s broader, shooter-perspective account creates some uncertainty about “single function of the trigger,” this is a criminal statute incorporated into §922(o), and any lingering ambiguity must be resolved in the citizen’s favor under the rule of lenity rather than expanded by executive interpretation. Allowing ATF to enlarge criminal liability by regulation would raise acute separation-of-powers concerns, effectively transferring Congress’s lawmaking responsibility to the Executive. This approach accords with our cases rejecting deference where Congress’s text does not clearly impose criminal consequences and insisting on clear statutory authorization before punishment may attach.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The statutory definition of “machinegun” in 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b) turns on whether the weapon fires “automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” and a bump stock, as a mechanical matter, still requires the trigger to reset and be actuated for each shot as the rifle reciprocates, making the government’s reading an extension beyond the best reading of the text. Because 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) and § 5845(b) carry serious criminal consequences, the Court should not allow an agency to expand criminal liability by regulation; where there is any real ambiguity, the rule of lenity and separation-of-powers concerns counsel against deference to the Executive. The Court has repeatedly emphasized that it has “never held that the Government’s reading of a criminal statute is entitled to any deference,” and “drive-by” deference in prior cases does not override that principle. ATF’s shifting interpretations over time further underscore the lack of a stable, historically grounded understanding that would justify treating bump stocks as “machineguns” absent clearer congressional authorization.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying the ordinary public meaning of 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b), a rifle equipped with a bump stock still fires one shot per mechanical “function of the trigger” because the trigger resets and is actuated again for each round as the firearm reciprocates; it therefore does not shoot “automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger.” Because 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) and § 5845(b) attach criminal consequences, ATF may not expand the statute’s reach by regulation, and any genuine ambiguity must be resolved in the defendant’s favor under the rule of lenity rather than deference to the agency. This approach is consistent with the Court’s insistence on enforcing statutory text as written rather than policy-driven reconstructions, see Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, 138 S. Ct. 1612 (2018), and with the skepticism toward deferring to agency interpretations in criminal contexts reflected in Whitman v. United States (Scalia, J., statement respecting denial of certiorari). On the statute’s text, the Final Rule is not a permissible reading of “machinegun.”

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 5845(b) defines a “machinegun” as a weapon that fires “automatically more than one shot … by a single function of the trigger,” and on the best reading of that text a bump stock does not eliminate the trigger’s repeated reset-and-actuation cycle; each shot still corresponds to a new trigger function, even if the device facilitates faster firing. Because § 922(o) and § 5845(b) operate in a criminal prohibitory scheme, the Court should be especially wary of allowing an agency to expand criminal liability by regulation, and any genuine ambiguity about “single function of the trigger” should be resolved in the defendant’s favor under the rule of lenity rather than by Chevron-style deference. The ATF’s shifting interpretations over time further counsel against deference, consistent with the Court’s skepticism of deference where the Executive “seems of two minds,” see Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, 138 S. Ct. 1612, 1630 (2018), and where inconsistent agency views merit less weight, INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca, 480 U.S. 421, 446 n.30 (1987). Given the practical consequences and the need for clear notice in criminal law, Congress—not the agency—must speak clearly if bump stocks are to be categorically criminalized as “machineguns.”
